utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are seated. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, madam. All the accused are here. From amongst the Defence teams, I only notice the absence of Mr. Meek. For the Prosecution, it's just Mr. McCloskey today. Mr. Butler is present all right. We are going to proceed with the cross-examination, and then we'll see where we get to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Before I ask a further question of Mr. Butler, I wonder if we could just go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Haynes. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I've done my level best to reduce the amount of questions I have for you to try and finish sometime today. This may involve a bit of corner-cutting, so bear with me. If we have to amplify, we will, but I want to turn to another topic now, which is really the creation of the Army of Republika Srpska. And as you have said in your reports and in your evidence, part of the composition of the Army of Republika Srpska were Serbian officers of the JNA who returned to Bosnia and joined VRS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you mean "Serbian," I take it that we're talking Bosnian Serb, ethnic officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And as I understand your analysis, you contend that those officers imported with them the rules of the JNA because they understood them and they had been trained in them and because they were the only rules available. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can we remind ourselves that throughout the time of the war in Bosnia, all sides were effectively fully mobilised; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would disagree with that, because I think one of the main contentions the VRS had during the course of the war is that until the civilian government declared an imminent threat of war in May or June of 1995, that the RS government wasn't in fact fully mobilising all of the available manpower and resources it needed for the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'll live with that, Mr. Butler. A document you were shown during the course of your examination-in-chief revealed that the numerical strength of the VRS was approximately 220.000 men. Does that ring a bell with you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly, yes, sir. I mean, I'm familiar with that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And of those, according to the document that was on the screen, about 14.000 had been officers or soldiers in the former JNA; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we're talking about the Utaga-92 [phoen] document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So of the manpower of VRS, about 6 per cent were former officers in the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, it would be right, wouldn't it, that the JNA officers returning or forming the Army of Republika Srpska tended to fulfill the offices from the top downwards?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That was -- that was actually by design. The VRS leadership, I mean, I believe correctly, you know, rationalised that by putting the experienced officers at the higher headquarters, that you could get the benefit -- or the best force multiplier for the limited amount of officers that you had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The effect of that was the Main Staff was almost entirely comprised of JNA officers, the corps substantially comprised of JNA officers, whilst the brigade had very few professional officers and the battalions virtually none at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is the practical reality of the policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And of course the battalions comprised the vast majority of the brigades' manpower?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we just briefly deal with the Zvornik Brigade, and I'm going to give you some figures. I can produce documents, if you'd like. I'd prefer not to because it slows things down. But we'll deal with the Zvornik Brigade. We've established through documents from other witnesses in this case that in July 1995, the Zvornik Brigade notionally comprised about 5.500 men. Is that a figure that rings a bell with you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you know how many of those men were former professional officers in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would -- probably -- if the number is 40, that might be on the high end. It might actually even be less. It's certainly not anywhere near an appreciable number, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, it was 14, 1-4.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1-4. Well, that would be a little low, but certainly under this context, I would accept that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Within the rules of the JNA, Mr. Butler, do you know how many officer positions there were in the Zvornik Brigade? I'm not going to expect you to be exact, but at least 20?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, easily a hundred, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, it was 388, in fact.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, platoon leaders and everything else, yes, sir, that's about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And do you know how many of those positions were actually filled by anybody, professional or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Under the circumstances --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll be fair.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- none, I mean, if even that. I mean, most of the platoon leaders and even company commanders were in fact individuals who had been mobilised from the enlisted ranks, so, I mean, I would be surprised if you had any appreciable number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'll answer the question for you. It was about 30 per cent were actually filled at all.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought we were talking about within the context of JNA. Okay, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, no, no, I probably phrased the question badly. I meant filled at all.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, vacant positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So of the five and a half thousand soldiers, 14 were former JNA officers, and only 30 per cent of the officer positions were filled by anybody at all. In organisational terms, the Zvornik Brigade was a million miles from the brigade as envisaged by the JNA rules, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, a fair characterization for Zvornik Brigade, and I think, you know, as discussed before, Bratunac Brigade and other brigades as well. It was a universal problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, moving on, I hope I don't mis-characterize your evidence thus far if I suggest to you you really offered us your opinions in two ways; firstly, you considered a rule or regulation and then you offered us your opinion as to its practical effect. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It does happen in context, so, I mean, I do take into account that certainly under the circumstances, that, you know, rules aren't going to be rigidly applied and that units and commanders are going to make allowances when necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: To borrow a phrase from Mr. Josse - I may have used a different one myself - your analysis of the rules and regulations of the VRS is thus academic rather than practical; you would accept that, would you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reflects what -- or what my goal of the analysis of the rules and regulations is that it reflects the framework, the common framework of the military organisation. I don't think I've ever made the contention that, you know, they were such -- so rigidly applied to defy reality. It's just a common framework how a military organisation runs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So certainly I make allowances for modifications, as necessary, by the battlefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just to clarify again a line that Mr. Josse took up, you've never spoken to the commander of the Zvornik Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you've never spoken to any of the assistant commanders of the Zvornik Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You've never spoken to the security officer of the Zvornik Brigade, nor the assistant security officer of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you've never spoken to a single battalion commander of the Zvornik Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I wasn't present for the battalion interviews, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, can you assist me, because I'm really not clear as to this. Is your failure to speak to those people of your choice or because of lack of opportunity? And I ask you that because of two answers you've given during the course of your examination in this case.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought you were going to explain what the answers were. The answer is: It's a combination of both. One, it's a practical aspect that, at least as far as the Office of the Prosecutor was concerned and its work in cooperation with the Republika Srpska, we did not have access to interviews of VRS officers until, the earliest was December of 1999, and then under very structured conditions. The second one is also a function of the practical ability of myself to, every time an interview mission was going down, to determine whether or not I needed to be a part of it at that nature. Given the first few years, the focus of the analytical effort was on the issues of corps command. Going out and participating in the direct interviews of battalion commanders of the Zvornik Brigade didn't seem to be a productive use of my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly make pauses between questions and answers, the interpreters ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I apologise completely to the interpreters. Mr. Butler, you and I are getting involved in a conversation here. We better go back to the more formal process of question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to read you the two answers which have perplexed me. Yesterday, you said to Mr. Josse, in cross-examination, the following: "I had a keen interest in talking particularly to those military officials who could provide information as to whether or not I was in fact pursuing a correct theory on the applicability of those issues. I mean, I felt that it was vital to my analysis to be able to get that opinion from these individuals." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: On the 21st of January, page 20059, in answer to a question by Mr. Ostojic, you said: "As a matter of practice in my reporting, as I've indicated in my reports, I was not prepared to be put in a position where I would be cross-examined on information that was derived from a witness who, by his position, would be testifying before this Tribunal. So within that broader context, my goal has always been only to use witness-based information when it was absolutely necessary to set the context of a particular event, so that my other analysis with respect to documents and with respect to other intercepts would make sense. The omission of witness statements by almost all of the parties involved was by design. It was not by a lack of awareness or any other information." Those two statements appear to me, Mr. Butler, forgive me, to be polar opposites. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your confusion, and I think maybe I can clarify it. The issue with respect to the witnesses and the crime bases, that is the issue where I did not want to talk to these individuals or include their material into the report, because that's a component part of the case. On the other end, I did -- with respect to the applicability of the rules and regulations, did want to talk to individuals, some of whom weren't necessarily even viewed as witnesses at the time for trial purposes, to confirm those. So while I take your criticism about, you know, what about talking about brigades and brigade commanders, I go back to the fact that, you know, to answer those questions, I did participate in interviews with General Andric, who was a brigade commander in the Drina Corps during the war, and with Colonel Trivic, who was also a brigade commander in the Drina Corps during the war and, as a course of those interviews, put forth the necessary questions to determine whether or not my analysis of the applicabilities of these rules were valid or not. So, I mean, maybe that's the proper way to parse it, I mean. I did make, you know, an effort to confirm with individuals who had significant expertise in these topics and whom at the time we would believe would have no reason to misrepresent anything to the Office of the Prosecutor, as they weren't directly involved in the case. I saw them as a neutral party by which I could ask these questions, and did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I may return to that with specific examples later, but I'm going to move on now. During the course of your testimony in the Blagojevic case, and for the benefit of others, it's page 4272 on Monday, the 10th of November, 2003, you said the following, and I quote: "In essence, unity of command is the general military philosophy that only one individual can be in command of one unit or of one series of units. You cannot have a function where you have multiple commanders in one unit. I think historically that approach has been found not to work effectively on the battlefield." Is that still your position?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, that is -- that is the principle that's embodied in the RS laws and in the regulations that we've talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The unity of command means this, doesn't it: Only one person can be in command of a unit at one time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I think we can qualify even further on what the JNA rules have to say about it, which is that the commander is the individual who has the sole right to command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The exclusive right to command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exclusive, well, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want to be clear about this in relation to my client's position. In the period between the 4th and the 15th of July, 1995, either Vinko Pandurevic or Dragan Obrenovic was in command of the Zvornik Brigade; that's right, isn't it? It can't be both.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. My view is that between the 4th and 15th of July, Colonel Vinko Pandurevic was in command of the Zvornik Brigade. However, the question which is part of these proceedings should presumably be: How much practical control did Colonel Pandurevic have to influence the day-to-day or hour-to-hour operations, given his proximity from his command and in light of the fact that Major Obrenovic, as his chief of staff, was functioning, in essence, as the deputy commander? My position, and I think it's well supported by the rules, is that Colonel Pandurevic does not officially relinquish command every time he leaves his brigade zone, but I certainly acknowledge that his material ability to manage to the degree that he would if he were there is somewhat compromised by distance and communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I understand your position, and again so that we're clear, your position as to who was in command is a theoretical one rather than a practical one; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, again, it's not that I haven't asked, because as the fact basis of this case revolves around, Colonel Andric, as the brigade commander of the Sekovici Brigade, found himself in the identical circumstances at the identical time of Colonel Pandurevic at Srebrenica, and so did Colonel Trivic, and when the question was put to them, did they consider that they were not in command of their organisations or did they somehow relinquish command of their organisations, both of those people, as the peers of Colonel Pandurevic, made it clear that they didn't view that they were relinquishing command of their organisation to participate in operations at Srebrenica. So I believe that in the both theoretical sense as well as the practical aspect of Mr. Pandurevic's counterparts, I'm on solid ground here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, that's a very interesting answer you give. Presumably, therefore, if you had had the opportunity of speaking to either the commander or the chief of staff of the Zvornik Brigade, and they expressed their view as to who was in command during that period, you would have factored that in and taken full account of it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir. But again, as a matter of practicality, again, I have to go back to the historical fact that the individual in question in this case, Colonel Pandurevic, was indicted prior to the RS government allowing the OTP access to these individuals. So while in the abstract it would have been a certainly wanted opportunity to interview Colonel Pandurevic, it wasn't an opportunity that technically could avail itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you've amplified your views on this topic during the course of your brigade command report, and it might be helpful now if we have a look at that. It's P684. It's pages, unhelpfully, 11 and 12 in the English and page 11 in the B/C/S, and we need to look at paragraphs 2.15 and 2.16.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm still on page 8, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, no, no, I was just going to check, as a matter of courtesy, Mr. Butler, if it was clear and big enough for you to read. I see you've got your glasses today.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 11 and 12, I thought that's what -- which paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 11 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise. What paragraph are we talking about, specifically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And 2.16. And 2.15 gives us: "A final component in the brigade deputy command and the JNA regulates the basis of responsibility and authority of the brigade deputy commander. This is not a singular position (as common in many Western militaries); instead, a position concurrently filled as part of the normal duties of the brigade chief of staff. In this function, the chief of staff has the authority, and the obligation of to exercise command over subordinates in the brigade where the situation warrants. However, in examining this 'command function' one must do so within the greater context of the roles and responsibilities of the chief of staff. In this regard, he is the principal adviser to the brigade commander and the primary facilitator through which the commander's intent commands," et cetera, et cetera. And we see, both at footnote 29 and 30, you cited authority for really the whole of that paragraph, paragraph 116 of what are the brigade -- are the rules of the brigade under the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I've got to slow down, apparently. Well, can we just have a look at that, that's P694 at page 64 in the B/C/S and 37 in the English. I'm sorry, Mr. Butler, this is where things slow down a bit. It's really the second half of that article we're looking at: "The chief of staff directs the work of the staff. He is also the deputy commander of the brigade. The chief of staff, in accordance with the commander's decisions, has the right to assign tasks to subordinates. The staff consists of an operations and training organ, an intelligence organ, a recruitment, personnel organ, organs for combat arms, and the office." Well, Mr. Butler, you were telling us yesterday how careful you were to accurately footnote your propositions, but whilst Article 116 certainly could lead you to the conclusion that the chief of staff is concurrently the deputy commander, it's quite a feat of interpretation, isn't it, to make the deductions you do on page 9 of your report on a mere reading of Article 116?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I disagree. I mean, you have to look at it in context of, you know, the same as 115, the brigade commander, when he's exercising that -- that same authority as the deputy. I mean, I don't see that this is a stretch at all, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, that may not be the kernel of the dispute between us. Can we go back, therefore, to P684 and look at paragraph 2.16. Thank you. "The functional empowerment of the chief of staff to issue orders as necessary should not be construed as an abdication or limitation of the commander's authority or responsibility. Rather, this authority vested in the chief of staff/deputy commander is designed to allow the timely and efficient issuing of orders or instructions necessary to facilitate the overall intent and directives of the commander or to deal with situations which require action when the commander is 'absent.'" Why the inverted commas around "absent," by the way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that was a function of just the limits of times PP. I would have put one single thing around it, but as you're aware, if you type in times PP the one character, you get a Cyrillic character. It's not meant to be a direct lift from anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right. Now, the footnote 31 refers us back to footnote 18, Article 10. We're going to have to hop back three pages in the document to find footnote 18, so if the court clerk could do that for us. I think we're looking for page 9 in e-court, so it will be page 6 in the actual report itself. So we need to go forward three pages from there. And I think we'll see that footnote 18 gives us the JNA Rules for Land Forces Corps (Provisional) of 1990; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So your proposition in paragraph 2.16 is derived from Article 10 of those rules, is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking footnote 18; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it says -- footnote 18 says "paragraph 65."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. You referenced back to footnote 18, under 2.16 --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: -- saying it was Article 10 of those regulations. Article 10 of those regulations is P412, page 7. Could we have P412, page 7, in e-court, please. That's apparently about operative disposition.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You really have me confused, because I'm not -- I'm not tracking here with you at all. Let me ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder whether he could be given a hard copy of his report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tracking through here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The proposition at paragraph 2.16 of your report is the functional empowerment of the chief of staff to issue orders, as necessary, should not be construed as an abdication or limitation of the commander's authority --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with that. I'm just trying to track through on the footnotes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. Footnote 31, supra, number 18, Article 10.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we're -- we're talking about a citing error. I think that's what we're wrapped around on, because this -- I mean, the footnote that we're tracking back to is the corps rules, and I don't think we're looking at those to -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: A technical error, would it be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I think we could identify it as a tracking error on the citation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So footnote 31 is in no way any sort of authority for the proposition you cite?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think what we're tracking back to is -- I think what we're talking about in 18 is a JNA Land Forces Rule provisional. I don't think -- so I suspect that, yeah, somewhere in the footnote transliteration, this one got mixed up. I think that seems to be the logical explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, can you help us, as you sit there now, as to what regulatory authority you have for the proposition you cite in paragraph 2.16?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, like I said, I would probably, like I said, go back to what we were talking about with the JNA corps rules, and I think that's -- if we're talking about cite 18 correctly, I mean, it's something I could check on. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, it's a bit late to be checking on it now, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I will acknowledge that if there's a citation error, obviously it's my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, at the time you wrote the brigades command report in 2002, I take it you were aware that there were indictments relating to substantially the same subject matter in existence against both the commander and the deputy commander of the Zvornik Brigade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly the commander. I'm -- I'm not sure about the deputy commander at that juncture, timing-wise. It may be the case. I just -- I don't recall exactly when he was indicted and how that worked out. I mean, it may very well be you're correct. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want to show me the day, I can confirm that for you or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We'll come on to something in due course that will confirm to you he must have been indicted by that stage, but --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, that's fair. I mean, I just -- it's been a couple of years, so, I mean, my memory is not exactly clear on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just before we leave that page of your report, glancing at 2.17, you cite there the interim provisions on the service in the Army of the Serb Republic, published on the 18th of August, 1992. That's a valid and legitimate source for looking at rules of the Army of Republika Srpska for our purposes, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's actually one of the few service rules that the Army of the Republika Srpska, on its own, did publish, rather than adopting the JNA ones in their largest extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, owing to your mistake, we've had to second-guess what regulation you might have been referring to, so let's see if we can find it. And as a preliminary to that, I'd like to ask you a few questions about other units in the VRS. There were regiments in the VRS, weren't there, artillery regiments? We have in this case the 65th Protection Regiment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's the unit that I'm thinking about, the 65th Protection Regiment. I think each brigade -- or certainly the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had an artillery regiment. I think there was a rocket regiment somewhere along the lines. So, yeah, I mean, in abstract, yeah, there were regimental formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Regiments were much more common in the JNA prior to 1995; you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, it used to be, as I recall correctly, the structure was the JNA at that time had an organisation that was along the lines of division, with regimental subordination, and then sometime during the mid-1980s they started to switch that to a corps and a brigade organisational structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And brigades and regiments were units of the same size, at the same sort of level, at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I've done a lot of research on infantry regiments, so, I mean, I will accept your word on that. I just don't know it's a fact. I just have not studied regiments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So what rules would have governed a regiment in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume that there would have been JNA regimental rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to give us an example to develop the point I made with you earlier, the commander of the 65th Protection Regiment was ...?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be Lieutenant Colonel Savcic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. So he was a lieutenant colonel, precisely the same rank as my client, who was a brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have 7D717 into e-court, please, page 6 in the B/C/S and page 2 in the English. And I'd like you to focus your attention on Article 17, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, these are the regulations of the brigade command authority in the regiment of the JNA, and they state: "In the absence of the commander, the chief of staff or the deputy commander stand in for him, with all the commander's rights and duties."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Command is a right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So the chief of staff stands in for the commander, with all the rights of command; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what that article says with respect to regiments, yes, sir. I'm kind of at a disadvantage because I don't exactly know what date we're talking about, so I can't particularly date this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to what I'm going to suggest to you is your mysterious Article 10. P410, please, into e-court, page 8 in the English and page 10 in the B/C/S, and these are the regulations on the responsibilities of the Land Army Corps Command in Peacetime of 1990. Is this P410? I think it might be P412 you've put up. Can we see P410. And I think we may need to go back a page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we had the particular one --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. You probably saw it quicker than I did, Mr. Butler. Go forward again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, we're on the right one, Article 10 right there, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: "The chief of staff shall replace the commander when the latter is absent and shall have all rights and duties."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did that apply to the brigade of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I mean, as I indicated before, you know, the phrase is defining "absent," you know, and as a practical matter, certainly the VRS was able to define "absent" when they wanted to, because you have the situation in July of 1995 where Major Obrenovic is the chief of staff, signing as the deputy commander or even still as the chief of staff; yet because of the extended absence of Colonel Pandurevic in August, suddenly he's signing it as acting for the commander, an entirely different role and function. So, I mean, maybe we're getting mixed up on the definition of what the VRS qualifies as "absent" with respect to the surrendering of command, temporary or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You've prepared reports in relation to each level of the Army of the VRS, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've prepared brigade report, corps, and Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what is it that makes the relationship between the brigade commander and his chief of staff unique, or is the relationship between the chief of staff and the commander the same at every level?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that certainly with respect to the corps and with respect to the brigade that the relationship is almost identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I only ask because on the 28th of January, in answer to a question from Madame Fauveau, you said the following, and it's page 20541, lines 8 to 15: "Would you agree that General Milovanovic, as the chief of staff, was the deputy commander of General Mladic because of the establishment; he did not need to receive any particular order to fulfill that position?" And you said: "Yes, ma'am, I agree. I mean, the inherent authorities that he had as the chief of staff of the Main Staff and as deputy commander meant that he did not need any specific order to function in that role when necessary." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but I don't -- I hope you're not suggesting that that same near commonality would apply to some -- an organisation like the Main Staff. I mean, the situation is a bit more complex at that level. I wouldn't agree with that, that it's the same as at a brigade command level. I mean, I think we're inherently clear with the fact that by position, the chief of staff concurrently functions as the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to reality and practice. And can we have a look at P417, the interim provisional service regulations of August 1992. It's page 21 in B/C/S and page 18 in the English. And we need to look at Article 60. "The hand-over of duties by commanding officers of squads, platoons and companies and the commanders of battalions, regiments, brigades and officers of the same rank, takes place in the form of a ceremony before the unit on parade." Were you aware from your analysis of witness testimonies of any formal ceremony and hand-over of the command of the Zvornik Brigade prior to the departure of Vinko Pandurevic on the 4th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that there was a customary parade that normally occurred prior to -- not just that deployment, for all deployments. I have never heard it characterized as a formal relinquishing of command. I mean, so, I mean, I can't agree with that characterization of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you ever consider, as part of your analysis, the interview of the sadly deceased Milan Maric? And perhaps to remind you, it's 7D72, page 9 in the English, lines 5 to 14, the same page in the B/C/S, 15 -- in B/C/S page 15 to 16.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What would help my memory is, is there a date associated with this interview, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. It's certainly within your terms of reference, Mr. Butler. It was at the 30th of June, 2002.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It begins, line 5: "DM" I assume is Dean Manning, probably says so at the bottom. "Now as Pandurevic is in the Srebrenica operation, who is in command of the Zvornik Brigade. This was made as a public announcement to all the troops in the morning session. It was said that Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic will take over from Pandurevic and will remain in command until the return." "When did this announcement occur and where?" "This announcement was made maybe on the 7th or 8th, when the troops were getting ready to leave for Srebrenica and they had their pulling out in the field, and just before they left the announcement was made that Obrenovic will take over the command." Had you considered that in -- before you gave your answer to this Court the other day?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I wasn't aware of it. But having said that, it doesn't change my opinion. I mean, I don't see this -- and I guess maybe the way that I can best qualify it is that if I were to accept your theory as to where you're going, it would certainly raise the question as to why Major Obrenovic, who is now commander, you know, would be signing all of his documents and material still as the chief of staff. It kind of raises the prospect that the only person who doesn't know that he is the commander during the period is the actual commander. So I have difficulty, under the circumstances, accepting your thesis because of that practical issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You have difficulty accepting the thesis that Major Obrenovic didn't know he was the commander; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, that's the logical extension of your argument, is that Major Obrenovic somehow is unaware that he's the commander and he's still peddling around as the chief of staff, and he never affords himself the opportunity to say, "Hey, I'm the deputy commander," or "acting commander," or no orders that note that formally. And then if you look at his actions down the intervening lines, particularly when we were talking about the situation in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade, I mean, he's frantically looking to get in touch with a commander, his commander, which he considers to be Pandurevic, not anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have 7D86 into e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 20th of May, 2003, and I imagine you had quite a deal of input into it. It's Dragan Obrenovic's statement of facts appended to his plea agreement.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, actually you're incorrect, I had almost no input into this whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, let's just read the one, two, three, four -- fifth paragraph down. Were you still employed by the Office of the Prosecutor in May of 2003 when Dragan Obrenovic pleaded guilty?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: "I acknowledge that I was in command of the Zvornik Brigade during the absence of my commander, Vinko Pandurevic, until his return at about midday on the 15th July. On hearing of this plan to kill the prisoners, I, as acting commander, took responsibility for the plan and supported the implementation of this plan." Do you still contend that Dragan Obrenovic didn't know he was in command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I believe what we're referring to in this context is Dragan Obrenovic does understand that, you know, he's functioning as the deputy commander, in his mind he is the authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think we better go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. We're moving on now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to say no offence taken, sir. I understand your --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, I understand you've been here a long time. It's a very tiring experience for both of us, but more so for you, because you've been sitting there for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I'm moving on now to another topic. I want to see if we can agree with a few propositions about the responsibility of the commander. The responsibility of the commander is for the units of the brigade and possibly for any further units subordinated to it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In short, the military responsibility of a commander is for men, or women, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not tracking what your -- for men or for -- I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, the responsibility of a commander is not and never can be for territory, can it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not necessarily true, but I certainly, within the context of what we're talking about -- I believe it's fair. I mean, Colonel Pandurevic's responsibility, you know, is to his soldiers, it's to his mission, whatever that mission will be, and in the context of that mission, whether or not he has terrain-related responsibilities or not is a function of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And not just to his men, but for his men?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, each unit of an army, whether in a defence, attack, or on the move, has an operational area for which it's responsible or a tactical area for which it's responsible?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, I understand it and, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And this includes the units of the JNA, whose rules describe operational responsibilities or areas of responsibility from its smallest unit up to corps level?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Not a quiz, Mr. Butler, but could you tell me the name of the smallest unit in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably think we're talking about a squad level, which is roughly six to ten or eleven. I mean, we may go down even lower, but I think a squad is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, I think we're on -- that's about as low as it goes. It's called an "odeljenje," which roughly translates to "squad." And the terrain for which a squad is responsible is literally marked out by the soldiers' boots; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, again, it's all mission dependent whether you're attacking, whether you're defending, things of that nature, but certainly at that individual level the territory that you're responsible is usually marked for you by your non-commissioned officer in charge, who says, "You here, you there."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But for our purposes, let's begin with the battalion of the JNA. You'd agree, would you, that the rules of the battalion described for it an area of defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And would you agree that within the VRS, the battalions retained the same terrain responsibility and area of defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, size, obviously, is going to be variable, based on terrain and by the number of soldiers that are available, but I guess the most important criteria is that at the battalion level, it's going to be the brigade commander who will identify those particular zones for the battalion. They don't pick their own real estate. The brigade commander would do that for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just to quite literally put it into evidence, I wonder if we could have a look at P2077, paragraph 320, at page 99 in the English and page 172 -- I'm sorry, page 100 in the English -- no, 99 in the English, page 172 of the B/C/S. I dare say it's a little while since you've had a look at this, Mr. Butler, so take your time to read it through.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just so that we have a practical illustration of that, can we have a look at page 172, the diagram of that principle. I'm warned I might be one page out. It may be 173. No, it's 172, obviously, or is that English? It's 100 in English, but the English is pointless. We might as well just have the B/C/S, 173. That shows how a battalion should organise its area of defence, and how the company should be arranged, and gives the dimensions of the front it should achieve, and the depth, and how it should position its artillery, its command post and the like. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We would call this a doctrinal template. It kind of reflects what it would look like in the perfect world, without any considerations of terrain or other battlefield issues. So, yes, sir, that's a fair characterization.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I think we're probably coming to the moment you've been waiting for, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The break?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. I'm with you on that one. But just prior to the break, let's have a little look at the map we've got behind you. The Zvornik Brigade attempted, as best it could, to arrange its battalions in that sort of formation. In fact, the battalions of the Zvornik Brigade were strung out along a confrontation line principally with the 2nd Corps of the Bosnian Muslim Army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't know if you've ever seen a map like that before that set out the areas of defence of the battalions. Were you aware of those positions in doing your analysis or carrying out your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I've actually -- I have seen map graphics that have what I believe is an accurate representation of those battalion positions in July of 1995, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, PW-168, who was on the ground, examined that map and eight others and confirmed that they accurately depicted the defence positions of each of the battalions of the Zvornik Brigade in July 1995. Do you have any reason to suppose that he's not correct about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only -- the only thing I would note is it's somewhere -- I think it's around 18/19 July, the former 8th Battalion, which was deployed down in Bratunac, comes back into the zone, so I'm not sure if that's accounted for or not. I don't even know if that's relevant for what you want to discuss, but I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, no, no. Thank you for that, it's very helpful. Within the meaning of the brigade and battalion rules, there was a difference in terms of terrain responsibility between the battalion and the brigade, and we need to have a look at the brigade rules now, P694, pages 19 and 20 in the B/C/S and pages 6 and 7 in the English, at points 12 and 13. Again, Mr. Butler, you know, I'm not here to trick you or take you by surprise. Take your time to refresh your memory of those provisions, which you may not have seen for a little while.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And we can see from that that under the rules of the JNA, the brigade was assigned a zone of operations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the zone of operations could take, I suggest to you, really three forms. It could be a zone of defence, when the brigade was in defence; a zone of attack when it was in attack; and a zone of march when it was on the move. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I would -- I would catagorise that as fair under the -- the JNA rules. I mean, you're obviously going to have static positions or logger positions or things of that nature, but I think we're fair on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just glancing back at the map, given, as it were, the position of the brigade and the combat disposition of its battalions, effective command -- or the effective command post of the Zvornik Brigade, in terms of its defensive operations in 1995, was the IKM at Delici rather than the barracks in Zvornik; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I mean it is -- it is the function of the forward command post to control the immediate fight, so that's -- that's a fair characterization.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I want again to -- it may be a cultural thing, Mr. Butler, but where I come from, we invite people who are experts to review evidence that we've heard and see what their opinion is on it, so I'm going to invite you to review some evidence that we've had in this case that you may or may not know about and see whether you agree or disagree with it. The area of defence of the Zvornik Brigade would be the deployment of the subordinate units in the territory on the ground where they were deployed, and that was PW-168 on the 10th of October, 2007, page 1613, lines 3 to 22. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, because I'm not sure exactly what the particular witness is -- I mean, are we referring to the static battalion locations, for example, on this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. He spent quite a lot of time looking --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, so, in part that's correct. I mean, I don't believe it's correct in totality. I believe in part it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I think you and I may come to an agreement and I may come to the realisation that I've wasted man-hours over the course of the last 18 months, but we'll see. Anything outside the combat disposition of the brigade units is not within the zone of defence, Miodrag Dragutinovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Martinovic"] on the 14th of June 2007, page 12654.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would disagree with that, based on the demonstrated behaviour at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: "The brigade has jurisdiction only in the zone of defence and within the combat disposition of its units and in buildings that were requisitioned for the purpose of the Zvornik Brigade. Everything else was under the authority of the local civilian authority." Again, Miodrag Dragutinovic, the 14th of June, 2007 at 12658.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially agree, and I think that the difference is that a recognition of that there is a difference between the zone of defence and a recognition of a combat disposition of units, which we know in July of 1995 there were a lot of Zvornik Brigade units running around a lot of real estate that didn't necessarily fall in those zones, so that's why as long as we distinguish that, I mean, it -- he's correct. I mean, where the Zvornik Brigade is actually conducting operations, it's in their zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: "When we are talking about the brigades, I read in the rules of the corps operative and strategic components, the corps and the Main Staff, there is a zone of responsibility. When we are talking about the brigades, there is no zone of responsibility." PW-168, October 2007, page 16109.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir. In the context of the JNA doctrine, that makes sense. I mean, it's envisioned that within the context of a conventional fight, your brigades will be doing your active combat operations, they will be given a designated axis or zone to operate in, and at a point in time when they need to be replenished, brigade's going to be pulled out and a replacement's going to move in to its place. A corps is not envisioned to be such a dynamic organization and in that context -- you know, a corps is going to be expected to operate on the same real estate for a longer purpose for a wider variety of reasons. It also recognises that within the context of a corps, you have a number of logistical or other organs that have to perform their missions and are not tied to terrain, they're in fact tied to where other people are on the battlefield or other functions on the battlefield. So, again, we can't keep looking at this in the context of an infantry battalion because it's not a fair characterization of a commander's full range of responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I've got time to conclude this particular topic before the break, particularly because one of my colleagues would like to raise a procedural matter before the break, so I will sit down now for a little while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. Josse. Do we need Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It involves the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. What's -- are you giving Mr. Josse orders?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I just wanted to direct your attention at page 36, line 11, it stands -- or, rather, there is a last name mentioned there which was transcribed inappropriately. It is "Martinovic." At line 18 of the same page, both the first and last name are wrong. Instead of "Mirodrag Dragutinovic," it says "Drago Martinovic." Could we please have that corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sarapa. Mr. Josse, please, we've very few minutes and I have an appointment at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it needs to be dealt with now. It involves the documents that the witness promised yesterday. I understand there has been some conversation between him and the helpful court staff, and I think there may be a suggestion that Mr. McCloskey and I see him at the next break in the presence of someone from the VWS for these documents physically to be handed over. So long as we don't engage in any conversation with him, I hope the Chamber has no objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would just -- for my part, I think I can dispose of the issue rather quickly. It's just I just need to confer with counsel on both sides to make sure that what I think is a naming issue which has been causing confusion, to make sure we're actually talking about the right name. Once I get that squared away, I think I can dispose of confusion real fast on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Butler. Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's the other issue involving the sensitivity of document issue, and I may need more communication with Mr. Butler if he is to identify if anything he's referred to goes to a sensitive nature portion of an exhibit, and that was part of what he was looking for. It would be very brief, but I think it's important to protect the interests of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I could be present for that, then there could be no possible objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have an objection to Mr. Josse's presence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I would appreciate his presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would have thought so. So that solves the problem. We authorise this meeting. You need to be present as well. I don't need to state that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we reconvene in 25 minutes' time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, Mr. Butler, to start this session with an announcement, I think we're making very good progress, you will be pleased to know, and I'd just like to regroup on the topic that we were dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let's be realistic, Mr. Butler. If there had been an incursion by the enemy into the municipality of Zvornik, it would have been a unit of the Zvornik Brigade that was tasked to deal with it, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in almost all probability, I mean. And even if the police were involved, they would be doing it under military control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. And the Zvornik Brigade drew its name from the town or the municipality from where most of its foot soldiers were drawn, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that was the custom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And so over and above, as it were, the area of defence on the front, the brigade had a general responsibility to defend the civilians who lived within that area from enemy attack?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe that's a fair characterization of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I probably telegraph this. There may not be too much daylight between us. To that extent, the Zvornik Brigade had a responsibility for that zone, to defend people within it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And so when we talk in terms, as you have from time to time done, of the zone of responsibility, that's an incomplete phrase. What you really mean is the zone of responsibility for combat operations, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that the term of art doesn't exist in the JNA doctrine to that -- to that extent, I do agree that it is a fair characterization of what we're actually talking about and actually saw on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much indeed. Just a few other things. A battalion did not have any, as it were, zone of responsibility to the same extent it had an area of defence as defined by the rules, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, we talk about the issue of schools in the battalion zones, and we say that in the context of, you know, in the proximity of where those battalions are operating. There is not, to my knowledge, fixed geographic points of a rear boundary that, you know, "This is your specific zone." So, I mean, that's when we talk about the issue of zones, what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, that's led neatly to my next question on the topic, and that is that PW-168 examined a series of similar maps to that and indicated the position of each of the schools that are relevant to the Zvornik area. I don't know whether you want to look at the maps, but he indicated that each of the schools was outside the areas of the battalion's defence areas. Would you agree with that, as described on that map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, they -- I mean, again noting what we're calling battalion defence area, that is correct, those schools would be behind the lines, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And lastly on this topic, I'm -- this is quite a long quote, so you might like to either listen to it carefully or watch it on the screen. I want to see if you agree with this proposition. It was a question from the President of the Court to PW-168, and it was on the 10th of October, 2007, at page 16137, lines 16 to 25. And the President asked: "Now, we are talking of an area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade which, let's imagine, is within those red boundaries. ." And if you glance behind you, you'll see he did join some dots on the map: "Not to complicate it, there is a building in there which is not administered or held or controlled by the Zvornik Brigade. Crimes are committed in that building by people who are not part of the Zvornik Brigade. Do you attribute any kind of responsibility to the Zvornik Brigade for crimes committed by people who are not members of it and having committed them in a building which is not under the control of the Zvornik Brigade, or would you say that the Zvornik Brigade is completely alien to such activity?" And he replied: "Your Honours, I think that in the situation as you put it, it would not be the responsibility of the commander of the Zvornik Brigade." Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I concur with that with respect to it would not be his responsibility for actions of soldiers under his control and of certainly which he would have had no knowledge, so I think that's a fair characterization of that. I can't see how a commander would be held accountable for that under that scenario. There are obviously other things that go -- involve at what point in time does the commander find out and what actions are taken, but I don't think that's part of what we're looking at here, so I do agree with that. The key issue is the fact that it's soldiers not under his command or control and a facility by which he has, you know, absolutely no authority or control over. I mean, those are the key qualifying points.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that's really all I want to ask you about the question of zone of responsibility, and you'll forgive me this comment. It seems that I may have started conducting this case thinking there was more distance between you and I than in fact there is. But can we move on to the relationship, please, between the brigade commander and his security officer. Let's look at what you know. In October 1994, an instruction was written and sent to the brigades; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, are we -- we're talking about the Main Staff instruction?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I am. And it dictated the way that the security and intelligence organs operated?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, just as a preliminary, this -- it was a directive to the security and intelligence organs, which were united as one service at the Main Staff level in the VRS; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And they were subordinate to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through General Tolimir, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Of course. I'm sorry, I didn't mean that to sound the way it did. But that was not the system under the JNA, was it? In the JNA, there were two separate services, a security service responsible to the Ministry of Defence, which was a civil organ, and an intelligence service responsible to the General Staff, which is a military organ, and that's the system common throughout the rest of the world, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly can't comment on the rest of the world, but certainly I think with respect to what we're talking about, within the SFRY Armed Forces there were parallel organisations, one dealing -- you know, one serving the civilian branch of the armed forces, I think it's working with the SSNO, and one that was involved with dealing with the issues of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So in looking at the security and intelligence service or organ of the VRS, through the regulations of the JNA, we have to bear in mind it's a fundamentally different organisation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, certainly within the context of where the Yugoslav National Army had a well-developed civilian infrastructure that operated under the Ministry of Defence, which dealt with many of those issues and was in fact -- the Ministry of Defence was an active decision-making authority for that. You do have to contrast that with the VRS, where, you know, in 1992, you know, the Ministry of Defence existed perhaps in name only and was in no way able to assume any of those other functions. So, I mean, the VRS had to do double duty in many respects, not only within the military context, but also deal with the issues that would normally be under the military/civilian apparatus of a government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I don't know the extent to which you're qualified to deal with this, but there are very good reasons, aren't there, for keeping your security and your intelligence services separate, because to combine them in one body really creates an extremely powerful body?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly within the context of the former JNA, where, you know, you did have to deal with the socialist apparatus and the inherent political structure, there -- there was never going to be, at the political level, you know, the desire to want to create a body that's so strong that one day it wakes up and decides it should be in control. So it is a function, in large respect, to those types of communist or socialist governments and, to a lesser extent, Western governments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You took the words right out of my mouth, Mr. Butler. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although, arguably, in my country, some days that's a disputable concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So when we look at the document, which I'm going to have in e-court in a minute, P2741 - can we put it up now - we do have to bear in mind, don't we, that things have changed radically since the JNA rules were written, in terms of the organisation it's directed to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, sir. I mean, when we look at these rules -- and again I qualify them always as foundational, you know, we have to keep in mind that these types of rules, these types of issues, were designed to be implemented by an army operating under a coherent manner, in a way that it was planned and structured. No military plans for the day that their country disintegrates into civil war and everyone says, "Oh, here's the backup plan in case we all fracture," you know, "What do we do next?" So it is to a large extent taking what you know and trying to apply it to a particular situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you'd mind just considering with me again instruction number 2, and in particular the second paragraph of that instruction.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you help us as to what the second paragraph of that instruction signifies to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to State Security Department?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, are we talking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's easier if I put the question. This instruction grants powers to the security and intelligence organ of the VRS, analogous to the State Security Department; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They're authorised to act and work on a task in their field analogous to the authority of the members of the RS State Security, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And correct me if I'm wrong, but that was a novel power, wasn't it; it was not something they'd ever had before?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the JNA or VRS, I mean, I think what -- we're reading this along the lines is the idea that while the -- with the RS MUP being empowered to conduct its own investigations and limited powers of arrest for these types of things of that nature, that you wanted to see a parallel ability to conduct those same types of investigations as the RS MUP. I would disagree that they didn't have that the same power before, because I would think that certainly those security members, operating at the highest levels of the JNA or at the SSNO, would have had those same types of investigative powers and ability to implement decisions on arrest. So, I mean, I don't think that these are unique powers that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm not suggesting they're unique. I'm suggesting they're new and additional. Would you agree with that? I mean, perhaps the foundational question is whether you are familiar with the authority of the state security system to act.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, I am; certainly not specific, but I don't read it as that. I read it along the lines of that it's a reminder that these individuals are entitled to act up to that level. I don't -- I don't believe that at this point where an instruction -- in the instruction this is a new power being granted. Now, having said that, I mean, if there's -- I mean, that's my opinion. If there's evidence that suggests otherwise, I will certainly entertain it, but I don't -- my understanding is that wasn't the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, let's put it this way: In practical terms, in relation to the Zvornik Brigade, which is the only brigade we're concerned with in this trial, you have no information that would lead you to believe that this instruction was not acted upon in a way that led to additional or extended powers, do you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, I think the practical aspect of this application, when it hit the ground, at least as far as the security branch people were concerned, it was a reminder of the fact that, you know, they needed to get out of their office and they needed to stop playing with the MPs, and they needed to start engaging in this type of work to this type of level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thanks. Now let's move on. You've been shown a number of sets of regulations both by Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Bourgon which related to the security and intelligence organ or organs. Some of them were available to you when you prepared your analysis and some were not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe that Mr. Bourgon did show me one document which was not available to me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In relation --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A JNA manual, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Can you tell us how many of those sets of regulations were available to brigade security officers in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no way of knowing that, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I know that when we got there in 1997, they had a -- a fairly complete set, and I know that a number of those were taken from other locations associated with Zvornik as well, but, I mean, I can't speak for what their state of library was in 1995. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So, I mean, it comes to this, perhaps a point I've already made: You've got no idea to what extent, in practice, those regulations that you were referred to impacted upon their work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The idea that I have, in practice, is the reflection of those activities that we see in the broader body of documents. So, I mean, that's where I base my, you know, opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how many documents have you reviewed from the security organ of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a long time. I wouldn't be able to hazard a number at this juncture. I mean, I -- I mean, I can give you anecdotal documents that I remember that came out of those types of places, and I think some of these have even come before the Court, but I just couldn't hazard a guess on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, just to put a point -- use an inoffensive example: Do you have any information to say that Milorad Trbic ever read the rules of the security organ or the instructions or methods to be employed by security officers, or any other JNA booklet concerning the security organ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if that question was ever raised to him or not, so I don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of the security training of the security officers in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, actually, because one of the documents that is out there is -- and if I'm getting the date right, it's a late 1993 document which does in fact list out the issues of security and how they were to be applied to the battalion officers. So, I mean, I have seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, therefore, based on your interpretation of the rules, as opposed to any direct evidence you have from those who operated them, I wonder if you could deal with a few questions. In the terms of paragraph 1 of these instructions, who was it that determined that a security officer's work was to be classified as counter-intelligence rather than anything else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, the instruction originates from the Main Staff, so, I mean, they were making that determination as to what they viewed the tasks were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, I mean on a day-to-day basis, in practical terms.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, in practical terms, yeah, the person who would be making those day-to-day decisions would be the security officer, Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
