utterances.text: Within the terms of that instruction, hypothetical, I know, but if a security officer committed a crime whilst engaged on what he determined to be counter-intelligence work, would the security officer be under any duty to tell his brigade commander about it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess that entirely depends on the context of the crime. If he committed a crime, you know, let's say in be abstract, if he committed a crime that involved the unlawful wiretapping of an individual that he thought was a suspect, I don't think that that would be something along the gravity that he would report to his brigade commander. That would -- if he were being a conscientious officer, would go up through the security chain. Conversely, if he were effecting an arrest or something like that and it involved the physical beating of a suspect or something of that nature, you know, I think that's an issue that his brigade commander is going to want to know about, and it would be expected he would report to that. So, I mean, that's an entirely situational-dependent issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I have to ask you this: On what basis do you come to that opinion, if your theory is based entirely on a reading of the rules?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I always try and default back to the idea that these are professional military officers and as a part of their obligations, that they're going to try and carry out their duties and their roles and responsibilities within the light of how they're there. I don't take the default value that as professionally-trained officers, these people are going to operate in a way that I would give credit to somebody like Milan Lukic, or Arkan, or somebody of that nature. I mean, I give them the benefit of the doubt based on their professional expertise and experience. So that's why when I say -- you know, that's my basis for making that. I mean, I make the expectation, perhaps wrongfully, and I certainly will be corrected on that where I have to, that by and large, these individuals are doing their best to do the duty as they understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, at least we know the basis upon which you opine in that way. If a security officer or his deputy, for that matter, needed assistance, in terms of manpower, in carrying out counter-intelligence work, where would he get it from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it were an immediate need of manpower that didn't require, you know, specialised purpose, I mean, presumably his first port of call would be the military police company commander. I assume that, you know, we're not talking about he needs individuals who can do detailed surveillance work or things of that nature, so, I mean, it might very well be from his superior, Popovic. It depends on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It would follow, wouldn't it, that if he wanted to use military policemen for counter-intelligence work, he would be obliged not to tell the commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely. If he were going to use military intelligence police for counter-intelligence work, for a task that's going to take them away from an already pre -- another order or another issue, I agree he wouldn't tell the commander he has to take him away for counter-intelligence work, but he's going to have to tell the commander that, you know, "I need to use these military policemen for a function, for a certain amount of time, that's related to my competence." You just don't wander over and pick the guys up. So, I mean, there is a practical aspect to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I follow that, but once he'd been allowed to pick the guys up, their purpose would have been his business and his business exclusively, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, within the field of counter-intelligence, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Which he, himself, determined?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, just to revisit briefly a couple of questions you were asked the other day, I just want to go back, and forgive me if it is a question that you feel you've been asked before. But how is it that you interpret the words in this document that forbid the commander from determining the legality of the work of the security officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which -- are we with the same document that's still up on the ELMO? I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Where -- where I interpret that is the phrase that's in paragraph 2, you know, with regard to the professional activities, you know, they are centrally controlled by the security and intelligence organs of the superior command. I mean, I think that's -- and you take the next sentence there, their full independence with the implementation of intelligence, counter-intelligence and operative tasks, so, I mean, I think that's where I derive that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think perhaps we need to look at another paragraph of the instruction. I think it's paragraph 7. So we need to go over two pages. Yes, it is paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, that's -- that's fairly clear right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, help me. What does it mean? What does it mean, that --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how to amplify. It means what it says. I mean, you know, monitoring the professionalism, legality and correctness of work in the organs is exclusively -- is carried out by the first superior, except for the part of their engagement relating to command and staff affairs. I mean, I think we've beat that one to death, haven't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Maybe. Mr. Bourgon asked you the other day a question, and I'll give the reference, January the 24th, page 20348, he asked you this question: "But let's get away from that scenario. I'm not talking about that scenario at all. I'm talking about any other scenario, other than this one. Can the commander still take disciplinary action after consulting the superior technical officer?" And your answer was: "Yes, if the superior technical officer concurs with the commander's assessment of the situation and the discipline that he wants to invoke, assuming the technical officer agrees, the commander can take those actions, yes, sir." You were describing a system where if the brigade commander became aware of illegal behaviour by his security officer or, I suppose, his deputy security officer, would have to go through the security officer higher up in the professional chain; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, just suppose this: Suppose a brigade commander was informed by his chief of staff and deputy commander that in his absence, crimes had been committed by his security officer and his professional superior, what realistically could the brigade commander do in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think his most realistic course of action is going to be he's going to be sitting in his -- his corps commander's office, explaining that situation. I mean, the fact that -- the fact that he is limited with respect to raising legal charges, I mean, and let's put words to the -- to the hypothetical here. Colonel Pandurevic encounters that situation and he wants to, you know, raise charges against Drago Nikolic, he's going to obviously have to go to Colonel Popovic first. If Colonel Popovic either non-concurs or Colonel Popovic himself is involved in this, Colonel Pandurevic's actions doesn't stop. His next port of call is his corps commander, and we go up that same issue. You involve your next superior operational commander, and your next superior operational commander starts to get involved in why his security officer may have been involved in this. And if we don't -- you know, and we go to the next operational commander, Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, that's how it would work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So his course of action would be to report the matter to his corps commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder if we could have P334 in e-court, please. English, page 2; B/C/S, page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is an interim combat report of the 18th of July, sent by Commander Pandurevic to his corps command or his corps commander. "It is inconceivable to me that someone who's brought in 3.000 Turks of military age and placed them in schools in the municipality, in addition to the 7.000 or so who've fled into the forests ..." Isn't that Colonel Pandurevic doing precisely what you describe?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I mean, that's one interpretation, and I would have to tell you it's certainly not an interpretation that his corps commander at the time would acknowledge that it is. Whether -- I mean, there's an open interpretation, obviously, as to whether or not at this point he is basically trying to euphemistically say, "And, yes, somebody killed them," that he didn't know about the plan, or that he was aware of the plan and that his -- you know, he's just upset about the way it was implemented, not the fact that it was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think I'll settle for, "Yes, that is one interpretation."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again, I mean, unfortunately, it's not an interpretation that his corps commander shares.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, and I know it's not one you share, either.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, but my opinion doesn't matter on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, that's why you're here. Just while we're on that particular topic, can we go back to a document we discussed yesterday, which is P329, and could we have that just briefly into e-court? I imagine you dream about this document, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: More so than you probably even realise, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's an experience we share.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've got a -- I've got a long-head start on you on this document, sir, I can assure you of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's just a simple couple of questions on this. It's your evidence, I believe, that in communications, VRS officers and soldiers used certain euphemisms to refer to prisoners of war in and around this time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly on the unsecured telephone network, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I believe it is your further evidence that they did this pursuant to instructions from somebody.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, say --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, they were told not to --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, not to discuss -- not to discuss sensitive --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In your analysis of the documents, have you found any other written report which refers so explicitly to the identity of the people detained as these two examples of Vinko Pandurevic's writings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not until the -- setting aside hospital documents and things like that, in a command document it would not be until the 23rd of July, where the Zvornik Brigade starts asking the question, "What do we do with the prisoners that we've been capturing?" So, I mean, these are -- I agree, they're extremely explicit documents in what they describe with respect to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. Now, a document analyser could draw certain inferences from that, couldn't they, Mr. Butler? And I'll put them to you for your comments. They could draw the inference that Vinko Pandurevic may never have heard that he was not supposed to talk about prisoners, let alone write about them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a -- that's certainly an open option, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And they may also draw the inference that Vinko Pandurevic didn't know that someone was putting prisoners in the municipality of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is completely speculative. There's a -- there's a hundred ways different people might talk about anything. We don't need the Court -- the Court, I don't think, is assisted by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. There's going to be an application to put this man's report into evidence in which he purports to interpret what was in my client's mind when he wrote these documents, and I think it's right that he should be cross-examined on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no objection to that, but the particular question, as it's asked, "Could somebody possibly say this or that," you know, anything is possible, I'll agree with that, but that doesn't move the ball forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, there's a simple solution to this. The question -- let me block it here first. The question was whether they may also draw the inference that Vinko Pandurevic didn't know that someone was putting prisoners in the municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and I think I can clear that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think you can answer that, because what you're being asked is not to speculate, but to confirm or deny whether such an inference could be drawn, and I think you are in a position to answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and in fact it was by me at one time, it was openly held open by me and my analyst that that was a possibility that what we were looking at, with respect to this 15 July 1995 order, was the first mark in the sand that Vinko Pandurevic gains an awareness of these prisoners in his area. I -- we -- I certainly, and my analyst, we certainly never -- you know, given the fact that Vinko Pandurevic was not present in the zone, we don't give him historical basis of knowledge on this issue. The 15 July 1995 combat report in large part reflects what he learned almost immediately upon returning to his zone. So we held that possibility open and then we -- you know, as part of the investigative process and as part of looking for material, we started looking for information that might confirm that as a working hypothesis. The problem that we had on that, from an analytical level, is -- and again it kind of leads back to the issue of does "asanacija" mean what we interpret "asanacija" to mean; is it possible that Vinko Pandurevic can be aware of the prisoners in his zone but can be unaware of the fact that they're being killed, given the fact that the same officers who would be telling them -- him that they're in his zone, you know, would those same officers be instructed not to tell their brigade commander about the fact that they're being killed? And you start to go along the lines where the plausibility of those theories starts to fall off to the side. I mean, I take it as an article of, you know, my respect for Colonel Pandurevic that, you know, he's recognised within the Drina Corps, and I'd argue the army, as one of the most competent brigade commanders of the war. This is a man, when you draft this report, you know, obviously understands the security implications of these prisoners and is rightfully wanting to know: Where are they? Are they under control? Do I have to worry about escape? He's taking these measures as a prudent commander. He may even be taking measures as a prudent humanitarian and taking the next step and saying, "Are these people being fed? Are their medical care being done?" Not because he either likes them or dislikes them, but on a practical sense. He's got to feed 3.000 more people. His brigade can't do that. Where is he going to get the food? Somebody in the staff has to deal with that. And so when we start putting all of these things together and look for evidence, that's where we start running into the problem. We're not seeing evidence of those types of inquiries. And that's why -- you know, it sounds great in the abstract and certainly is part of my own feeling of what Rule 68 meant, you know, we looked down these issues. And I guess in fairness to Mr. Haynes, I mean, not having to live through that process, it might seem somewhat invisible to him, but we spent months, if not years, going through these worm holes to determine whether or not these alternative readings of the document held any weight. And I hope -- it's a little long and I apologise, but I hope I was clear about where we went with -- on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, thank you very much. I want to move away from that, please, and just move to an entirely different area about which you were cross-examined earlier in the week. In terms of your analysis of this case, and to borrow your word, what was the visibility of Petar Salapura is relation to the detention, interrogation and execution of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the invisible man, so to speak. There is, I believe, one intercept that talks about him. Nobody else really talks about him in the context of individuals who've talked to him. And as I understand that as we've investigated, the information that we have come up with, at least in the early stages, is the fact that with the exception of one or two days, he wasn't even around there. So, I mean, he is the invisible man in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And to just remind ourselves, he was the Main Staff chief of intelligence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Svetozar Kosoric, what was his visibility in terms of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Svetozar Kosoric is Krstic's chief of intelligence. I mean, our ability to track that reflects that almost exclusively Kosoric was in the company of General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And Dusko Vukotic, the Zvornik Brigade assistant chief of staff of intelligence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's more of a questionable issue. Dusko Vukotic puts himself on a hill in Divic and spends days out there. Other people kind of put him closer to Standard at various points in time. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: An extremely broad question about visibility. That opens the door to the entire investigation, including statements of people who I've pretty much stayed away from, like Milorad Trbic. So I'm not sure these kind of broad, open-ended questions are, unless you want to go into all that, something that is -- is something the Defence wants to do, because it's opening the door to the other critical information that, for obvious reasons, I have stayed away from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment on that, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It wasn't Mr. McCloskey who ventured into this area that I want to deal with, it was somebody else, and I'll put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Whatever the rules may say, did you conclude that the intelligence service had little or nothing to do with the arrest, detention -- arrest and detention of prisoners of war in the area of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the exception of the one intelligence report reflecting the capture of a radioman from the 28th Infantry Division, there is very little information that I'm aware of that the intelligence organs of the brigade had any dealings with these prisoners of war in that area. So, I mean, I do agree with your -- with your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. That was really all I wanted to get from you. Now, moving on to an entirely different topic, in your evidence in the Blagojevic case, at page 4281 on the 11th of November, 2003, lines 13 to the end of the page, I'm going to summarise this and others can look at it, you told the Court that a brigade commander would be bound to follow a direct order from General Mladic, effectively skipping the corps level. Do you still stand by that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and I think we've seen practical applications of that. They're not -- you're not going to be in a situation where your brigade commander is going to turn around and say, "You can't give me that order, it only has to come from General Krstic," so that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in fairness to you, you went on to say that there would be a responsibility on the inferior officer, as it were, the brigade commander, to let his corps commander what he had been tasked to do when it was practicable to do so; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I mean -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: At a lower level, PW-168 told us that officers from the Main Staff could come to the brigades and give commands to brigade units without seeking permission from anybody. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, I think that's, you know, a complete distortion of the concept of effective and professional command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Have you anything -- any material that would cause you to be able to say that, in practice, that did not happen from time to time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I think as a matter of practical aspect, it probably would have happened from time to time. I mean, I can easily foresee a circumstance where, you know, a colonel is going to come to a lieutenant and say, "I need this accomplished," and this lieutenant is going to view this as, you know, an officer who's entitled to give the orders that he's giving. He's going to follow it. And, you know, if it comes to a point where it's impacting his previous mission that was done by his other commander, he's going to tell his commander about it, let him know that, "I've received these instructions to do this. Is this okay with you, sir? You know, you're my boss."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I suppose the sort of time when that might have occurred is when the commander was absent on another operation and the deputy commander was fighting ambushes 10 or 20 kilometres up the road and was not in radio contact.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one circumstance where it could occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you that there are actually provisions in the regulations of the Army of Republika Srpska that provide for this. And could we please have P417 placed into e-court, please. It's page 10 in both the English and the B/C/S. I apologise. I'm interested in, as it were, reading this backwards. There seems to be an illogicality in the order these rules as set out. But can we start with Article 17, which reads: "Members of the army shall carry out the orders of their superiors without demure, in full, accurately and punctually. If by any chance the order was not given in good time, the person is required to take measures and act in accordance with the specific situation. Members of the army shall carry out the orders of the most senior officer present when the superior officer is absent." Now, before we move on to the questions: These rules are rules of the -- the Rules of Service of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And if the average battalion soldier was aware of anything, these are the rules he's likely to be aware of, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just to complete the picture, these rules were in force in 1995 and carried on being in force until they were revoked in 1997. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware when they were revoked, but I certainly knew they were in force during the period that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you stop, Mr. Butler? I don't think we're not getting transcript at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It stops at the word "hypothetical."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are a hundred percent right --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mine's still running for some reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but it's running on the main monitor, it's not running on LiveNote, so we have that problem. Yes, yes, it's okay now. It has come on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, his answer, his reply --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go into private session just a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder if you could -- I can't actually remember what the question was now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I can go back to what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, I agree with the application of this, so I think, you know, you have a situation where you see it on 14 July where, because of the inability of Major Obrenovic to get in touch with his brigade commander or even his corps commander, you know, he does get in touch with General Zivanovic, who has no command authority at the time, but recognising the situation on the ground, you know, tells Obrenovic, "Take this as an order, here's what you've got to do." I mean superior officers, you know, are expected to do that. Now, taking it back to the issue that you raised directly, I mean, I'm not going to deny that I can't foresee a circumstance where an individual like Colonel Popovic or Colonel Beara is going to walk over to a group of soldiers and say, "Here's what I need you to do." I mean, they're going to -- they're going to say, "Yes, sir" and move out, draw fire. Where you start to stretch the boundaries of that is as you start working your way up the chain of command to officers who have the knowledge of both the powers and limitations of these individuals as well as the knowledge of what their orders are supposed to be, because these are the types of people who are going to start recognising the inherent conflicts here and are going to be the ones that have to deal with these conflicts. So, like I said, I certainly hold open that issue, but it is a sliding scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Of course. But as I began today, apart from 14 men, the Zvornik Brigade was comprised of five and a half thousand unprofessional soldiers, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but many of those individuals are part of the 14 men. People who acknowledge awareness of what's going on, to degrees, are the professional soldiers. I mean, understanding that he hasn't testified, you know, an individual of the calibre of Major Jokic, you know, isn't going to be ambiguous about what this all means. Even an individual like perhaps, you know, Captain Sreten Milosevic, Captain Milorad Jasikovac. You know, these are not the type of people who are going to be ambiguous. And certainly, you know, while your battalion commanders may be of lower level, they're certainly not uneducated men, and at a point in time when they start realising that the orders that are being given them, you know, are resulting in the machine-gunning and murder of individuals or detention in facilities that's plain wrong, you know, these people are not going to just blindly follow, in theory. They're going to, as responsible junior commanders -- you know, their first port of call ought to be their superior officer, either Major Obrenovic or Colonel Pandurevic at the time, wanting to know if this is what's really -- "what we're really supposed to be doing."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that's why I say, it's a sliding scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is that a military expertise you're using in giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's a military expertise based on, you know, my knowledge of the way that things were working in the Zvornik Brigade and the professionalism of the individuals in question. I am not, to be fair, trying to impart my potential military values on their system. I recognise that that's not a fair characterization and it certainly would be an unprofessional one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, can we go to Article 16: "When several units are given a joint task, a commanding officer shall be appointed in good time to direct the execution of the task. If this is not regulated beforehand, the role of superior officer shall be assumed by the most senior officer, who shall direct the execution of the task. If a unit or an institution is suddenly left without a commanding officer, command shall be assumed by his deputy or the highest ranking officer in that unit until a new commanding officer is appointed." Within the meaning of that rule, would you regard the movement of prisoners from Bratunac to Zvornik, involving, as it did, soldiers from different units, as a joint task?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And would you say that that rule applied in terms of who was in command of that joint task?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- in theory, with respect, what should have been happening was given that these were the joint tasks, your command entity would have been the Zvornik -- I'm sorry, the Drina Corps headquarters or an officer thereof who's exercising direction of that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But in the absence of that, the person who was giving commands to those soldiers to get on the buses, guard the prisoners, get the prisoners off the buses, would be the commanding officer, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm differentiating between the senior officer present and the commanding officers. I mean, are we -- you're talking the senior officer present?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To some degree, it would, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Providing again that the soldiers obviously would understand that it's in his competence to do these orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soldiers sitting in Bratunac and some strange officer comes up and says, "Get on the buses, you're going to Zvornik," you know, is probably not going to react to that. If it's somebody within their chain of command, they will react to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Or if it's a colonel, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a possibility. Again, it's situation dependent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, during the course of your evidence-in-chief, you told us that General Mladic convened a meeting of his senior brigade commanders at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters on the 12th of July. That's page 19869, lines 7 to 21, on the 17th of January. What is the source of your information for that assertion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that particular assertion, there are no documents, so in order to set the context, that is where I've had to rely on testimony or statements of individuals who were present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, let's not beat about the bush. An individual or more than one individual?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember certainly Colonel Trivic. Like I say, it may be -- it may be more than one, but I'm -- I'm just not recalling at this juncture. But I know Colonel Trivic did discuss this in some detail at some juncture.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm venturing to suggest to you that the only person you can have spoken to or place at that meeting on the 12th of July was Colonel Trivic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, because I believe that at some juncture, Captain Nikolic, the Bratunac Captain Nikolic, understood that -- you know, said that he knew that that was going on as well. But, no, as for the actual inside guts of the meeting, I think Colonel Trivic is the only person who's present to acknowledge the internals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But you were present at the interview of Momir Nikolic, and without going through pages and pages of interview, we can probably stipulate this as a fact: He said the meeting took place on the 11th of July, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You were present --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was -- look, he -- there are other discussions that he's had on the issue. I mean, I don't recall him saying it is the 11th of July. My information that it's the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you see General Krstic give evidence in his defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did he not refer to this meeting being on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I mean, I could stand to be corrected, but I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I was gone at that juncture.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Perhaps you'll take it from me. He placed this meeting on the 11th of July. Are you aware of what the discussion was at that meeting from, for example, the account of Colonel Trivic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the account of Colonel Trivic, the topic of discussion at that meeting was the initial planning process with respect to Mladic's decision to quickly move on to the Zepa enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And according to Colonel Trivic, did you understand there was any opposition to that plan?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe both -- you know, Colonel Trivic reflected that he had some opposition and that Colonel Pandurevic had some opposition, not necessarily with the conduct of the plan, but the fact that their units had been in the field for a long time and there was an open question whether or not, you know, they would be able to motivate them and get them to accept this next mission and move on with good order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And any other reason? I mean, didn't Colonel Pandurevic say at this meeting, according to your understanding, that it would be madness to go to Zepa when the whereabouts of the column was not known?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do recall that being attributed to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, by the evening of the 12th of July, we've -- it's clear from intercepts you reviewed, the direction and whereabouts of the column was perfectly well known, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that context, I think it was, you know, the fact that the column was out there and moving was known, but as I've testified before, there was a great deal of ambiguity about the size of the column and the potential military threat that it posed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The other thing was, and I'll have a document put into e-court here, please. Can we have P181 placed into e-court. And you will need to look or read it all through. But this is a document dated the 10th of July. It's from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. It's signed by General Ratko Mladic. And, in particular, I'm interested in your looking at paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Scroll down in the English, please. Thank you. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, according -- according to this order, the offensive on Zepa was to be commenced on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, only on that issue. And to be clear, in case, like I said, there's -- there's a need to be clear on why we're debating the 11th and the 12th, one of the things that I also take into account in these issues is that the officers in question also report that when they went from the headquarters to this meeting, that they drove through the UN compound on the evening 11th to get to this particular meeting. Now, I think there's plenty of evidence that the UN has noted that they weren't letting anyone through the compound on the evening of the 11th, they weren't disarmed until the 12th. So, I mean, I take that as part of the fact that maybe some of these officers are mistaking what particular day it was. Their remembrance of the context may be correct, but, you know, they weren't driving to this meeting through Potocari on the evening of the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Sorry, what officers? What officers say that and where?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that General Krstic says that, and I believe that General Trivic indicates that that was the path that he took.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you aware that General Trivic --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, not "General." "Colonel." My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Colonel Trivic referred to the fact that there was a meal during the course of this meeting, a celebratory meal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There was a celebratory meal at the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade on the 11th of July, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just told you I didn't believe so, so, I mean, you're asking me again?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And where was General Mladic during the evening of the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where he was on the evening of the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is that -- is that a serious answer, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, the answer is: I don't know. I mean, he's -- he had accommodations at the Hotel Fontana, but I can't tell you where General Mladic was on the evening of 11th July. I mean, I can track his movements through -- well, let's go back. The evening of the 11th of July would have been, what, the first meeting and the second meeting, so he was at the Hotel Fontana --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Let me get my dates right. The first and second meetings, he's on videotape, so he's at the Hotel Fontana until, what, 9.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So maybe longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And where is the Bratunac Brigade headquarters in relation to the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's down the road at the old ceramic factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Walkable?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What time did the meeting take place that Colonel Trivic told you about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, if memory serves, it's 10.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you remember Colonel Trivic telling you about General Mladic leaving the meeting, he had to go after the meal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that fact, but I certainly won't dispute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What time was the second meeting at the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, I'm sure I've got it in my report. I mean, we can go through the timelines on it. If you want, I'll look.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In essence, you rely on, for your assertion that this meeting was on the 11th rather than the 12th, on the witness interview of one man, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, I know everyone's getting tired, but you just reversed the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did I? I'm very, very sorry. I'm very sorry. I'll leave the point. I think the point's made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, when he said, "Everyone is very tired," he was suggesting that he is less tired than you are. Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We'll see when we get to redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: A wholly separate issue. On the 28th of January -- well, actually, I can -- I can cut this short. Can we just have a look at P110.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this document you want up is dated 12 July and you had preambled as 28 January?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I was going to refer to you some questions you had been asked on the 28th of January --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: -- but it's not necessary, Mr. Butler, to read back to you what you said previously. Just help us very, very briefly with what this document represents.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I think as I've testified, this is one of the manifestations of the work you see out of the various commands and staffs, who are scrambling around in order to get buses, in order to start moving the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can we now have a look at P156, please. Is that the first document on the page? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We can just confirm the first document is timed at 0835. This document is timed at 10.00 in the morning, an hour and a half after the first one. Help us as to what this document is. Who is it from, and who is it to, and what's it about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the commander of the Drina Corps to the Republika Srpska Main Staff and their associate -- their main command post, rear command post, for information. They're asking for additional fuel pursuant to the Main Staff commander's orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right. Now, it's no use doing this in English, so can we just have the B/C/S copy of this document on the screen, and there should be a second and third page to the B/C/S document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document has only one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document, from your past dealings with the documents in this case, and are you aware that attached to the back of it were a list of vehicles and registration numbers and indications of what fuel they'd been supplied with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I've seen the face of this document. I don't know that I'm aware of seeing the back end of the document. I mean, if you can show it to me, I can -- I can probably confirm that one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'll tell you what I'm going to suggest, Mr. Butler, because I'm very nearly done, that we have a break now and I can tidy this up in my last topic with you and then that will be over. I ask that respectfully, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that okay with you, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have -- one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this time the break will be of 30 minutes from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: On the last lap, Mr. Butler, so far as I'm concerned, anyway. I'm sure you're glad to hear that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm here at your disposal, gentlemen. I mean, it's part of the job, and I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: All right. Before I move to my last topic, I just want to ask you one question about your approach to the analysis of this case. Do you or did you ever admit of the possibility that a soldier of the Army of Republika Srpska might have been at a crime scene, either of his own choice or because of the orders of a high-ranking officer not in his chain of command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I certainly agree that that could be a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on now. And as a preliminary to dealing with this last issue, can you help us as to your understanding of precisely who Semso Muminovic was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of July 1995, I presume we're talking about, I think he was a -- an official with -- he was one of the brigade commanders of the 24th Infantry Division, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And your understanding of where he would have been located physically when he was talking to Vinko Pandurevic over the Motorola?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I wouldn't know where he would be physically on the ground at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right. I mean, just so that we're clear, and I fully understand that time has passed, but did you understand him to be somebody who was associated with the column or somebody who was associated with the 2nd Corps in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, I -- I associate him as an individual. He is with the 24th Division, obviously part of 2nd Corps Tuzla, but I don't believe he was ever in the body of the column. My understanding of his role is he was on the ABiH side of the lines and doing it from that juncture.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's fine. It was just something that you said earlier caused me to think you might have been confused about where he was. Now, at the time you wrote your initial reports, were there available to you personnel records from the Zvornik Brigade relating to July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe -- yes, we had them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I take it there were available to you the regular and irregular combat reports from July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, at least from the Zvornik Brigade. We didn't have the Drina Corps-related material at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to start, really, by putting back into e-court a document that you and I have looked at several times during the course of this morning. It's P334, the regular combat report of the 18th of July. And I really want to --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you characterize that correctly, because this is the interim combat report of 18 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, I mis-characterized it. Thank you for pointing that out to me.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm really only interested in paragraph 3, in which the dead and wounded are listed, and you will see that it lists that there were 27 dead people. And if we go over the page, 100 or so injured and 13 missing. Was that a document that you saw and considered before you wrote your report or gave your evidence in this or indeed any case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, although earlier I may have slighted overstated the number. I attribute it to 40. But I think my base of knowledge is also on the death certificate records. So, I mean, certainly, on July 18th, if he's saying 27 dead, I mean, I'm happy with that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, actually, it's rather less than that, because if we go to P321, on page 2 of the document in English, you'll see at page 7 -- sorry, paragraph 7 -- I'm mis-characterizing everything now -- that there are five men named there who apparently died in the combats around Srebrenica, who we have discovered were included in the figure of 27. So it's 22. Is that a figure you are happy with? If not, we can look at another document.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, yeah, I'll -- like I said, I don't think I've ever gone through each and every death certificate to parse that out, so I mean in that context, I mean, if you have guys have done that, that's fine. At face value, I'll accept your numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right. I mean, not to beat the thing to death, but that doesn't make it, does it, the most serious day's casualty in the history of the VRS, as was suggested to you by Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, and in fact I'm thinking that through a later date, I would probably say that the people in Bratunac might argue about that one, simply because they took a heavy hit at Kravica in January of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Quite.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I will acknowledge that that might have been an oversimplification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Quite. But the figure of 40 has come into your mind from somewhere. Do you recall where it came in your mind?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, as -- as a function of what I was looking at with the personnel documents and everything else, we had a number of the death certificates, the certifications of when soldiers died on the battlefield and what the circumstances were, that the battalions were required to fill out, so that at a point in time not only would certificates of death be issued, but it would be a way that the families could continue to claim any form of veterans' benefits. That is my understanding of what those documents were for.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear on that and we can chase that one to ground, 7D421, please. I'm not going to go through all of this, because it's a long document, but is that the document you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, but I can confirm that I have seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you can see that we've taken the trouble, during the course of this trial, to put asterisks by those who died on the 16th of July, and we've come to the figure of 23, I think. Have you always approached, as it were, the events of the 16th of July on the basis that 40 people or more died?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- the number to me is abstract. I mean, again, because of the focus of my analysis on this, the combat within the column, while a part of it wasn't relevant to what I was looking at with respect to the linkage to crime scenes, so whether it was 20 or 40 or more, I mean, I don't think that that would fundamentally change the character of my analysis. If there's a point to be made, certainly I'll entertain it, but at face value, I wouldn't see how that changes anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your assertion, I think, in evidence-in-chief was that the numerical superiority of the 28th Division was a major factor, as well as the losses he was suffering, in Colonel Pandurevic allowing the column to pass. Is that something you still stand by, now that you know that the dead are about half as many as you thought they were?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That -- that is a contested issue of how many are dead, and they're not including the police and the missing, and so I think to question that as a fact is not fair. I think he can put his position, but not as a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I may have to argue this in the absence of the witness, because I've put the missing figures into evidence, and it wasn't challenged in redirect. You've had your opportunity to challenge that, and I'll put it to this witness that the figures for missing people show one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, perhaps you can rephrase the question by making it clear that, in relation to the missing or what Mr. McCloskey has been complaining about, that this is your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to -- I'm going to go the long way around, given the objection. I'm going to ask that P2089 be put into e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no objection as he puts it to his case, but I don't think we're going to prove, with Mr. Butler at this late time, the number of casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, and I don't think that the question, as put, was categorically asking Mr. Butler to confirm with precision the amount of casualties. I think Mr. Butler was being invited to state whether he would be prepared to cut that figure that he mentioned earlier by a half if the contention of the Pandurevic Defence team is correct. That's how I understood the question, and of course you've argued that before, and you can continue arguing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is a document which was generated five years after the events of Baljkovica on the 15th of March, a little less than five years after, and it is the details of Bosnian Serb soldiers still missing. And, again, we've been through this with some care, and you'll see there's an entry at number 1 and an entry at number 4 of soldiers who disappeared on the 14th and 16th of July respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is this a document you've seen before?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So in making your conclusions about what motivations Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic may have had in letting the column go, you didn't know that in the final analysis, as we now contend, 23 people died and two went missing, did you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, but, I mean, maybe if I can get us right to where I think the issue is going on this, my analysis of the situation is done off of the basis that Colonel Pandurevic at the time is reporting up his chain. And I hope I've never done this in the context of my testimony. I mean, I've never made a conclusion whether or not his decision was justified or not. That's certainly not my position to make, even as another military professional. The point that I'm making is the fact is that on this is that Colonel Pandurevic, as a military professional, is arguably operating off of incomplete and potentially erroneous information, and he made the decision that he made based on the information that he had at the time. The fact that in the cold light of the peacetime world, everyone learns that it wasn't quite that way, is totally unsurprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's an interesting assertion. How many dead do you recall he reported up his chain of command on the 15th or 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that he gave a number in the 16th July in his interim combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right. Shall we have a look at it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. I mean, if he did, he did, but I don't recall the number there. I just recall the basic guts of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That would be P330. Can we have P330 into e-court, please. And we'll need to look at the second page in English, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In that report, there's apparently no awareness of casualties or fatalities at all, but that's an interim report, so --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree. Go back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Sorry, I might have missed something. Yes, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, about 10 dead. So, in fact, what we now know years later is that Colonel Pandurevic's comprehension of the situation is actually not as bad as it turned out to be; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, in the cold light of reality, yes, it may very well have been that way, but you're certainly not going to get a value judgement from me saying he made the wrong decision under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, but you have made a value judgement as to why he made it, haven't you, both in your reports and here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and I believe it's, again, not my value judgement, a reflection of the value judgements that he has sent forward to his superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, can you give us your analysis of what motivation there was on the part of the Muslim forces to agree to a ceasefire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the obvious motivation that I would understand would be that they wanted to completely withdraw from the territory with as little loss of life as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It seems both sides reached an agreement that suited their purposes, then?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly appears that way. Having said that, let's define "both sides." Is it at the tactical level? It didn't suit, particularly from the VRS perspective, it did not suit the objective of their leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I thank you for that answer sincerely, because of course I'm only concerned with defending somebody at the tactical level. Did you, in reaching your conclusions in your report or before this Court, ever consider information as to the state of the column, in humanitarian terms, on the 15th and 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I've ever done a detail analysis. I may have made comments about the fact that my understanding is with respect to percentage that were armed and issues like that, but I don't think I've ever tried to parse through walking wounded and things of that nature. I hope I haven't. I don't know the issues for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yeah, well, I'm going to give you the opportunity now if you never have because of course we want your analysis of things, and if there's new material, you should have it. Can you have a look at 7D234, please, at page 9 both in English and B/C/S. Does the name Sabic, Vejiz mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. So I take it this is a witness statement you haven't seen before.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I saw it, it certainly didn't register as something I'm remembering. I just -- I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, can we now go to page 9, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I'm looking at the very bottom of the page, and I think I'm going to have to read this into the record, because I don't think it's a document that is in e-court in B/C/S. But about halfway down the last paragraph, it says: "The men who were not injured carried us who were wounded back to the brow where we were before. It could have been around 1700 hours. I sent couriers to the forest where the rest of the column was to ask for some help, and around 50 people came to help us. After seeing what happened to us, the group that came to help us started to panic, and on that occasion they informed me that the rest of the column that was hiding in the woods was in a complete chaos. The people in the column had no more control of themselves. People were in panic and many of them were committing suicides. Ekrem Salihovic, a.k.a. Eka, reported this to me. "I concluded that it was now a question of minutes before the people in the column went completely crazy and Chetnik attacks were continuously going on. I suggested that we try to break enemy lines by ourselves as fast as possible and that help was coming from the other side (the BiH Army), but we couldn't wait for them anymore. We had no other option than to attack from our side in order to join our army on the other side. I tried to make a radio contact with the 24th Division, but the Chetniks would block any attempt." Did you understand that to be, as it were, the state which the column was in on the 15th and 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If that's going to be fair, he's going to need to be able to read the -- a bit more of that, especially if it's date -- date-specific, you know, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We can go over the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's fair enough, unless the witness is in a position to answer the question based on the knowledge that he has already amassed in his mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I can go back to the front page of the document, if you want, but it would only be to establish that this was a witness statement taken in April of 2002 so -- ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I mean, while I obviously, you know, have got a little bit of an uncomfort level taking one report and extrapolating it forward, I mean, this seems to be, in large degree, you know, a consistent story from what I understand that the conditions were in the column. It was in an extremely ragged state. They had not eaten and probably had very little fresh water for a number of days. But at least towards the front of the end of the column, I mean, they were still capable of conducting military operations and attempting to do so, to the limited degree that they had left. So, I mean, I think it's a fair characterization, and I wouldn't -- you know, like I said, I wouldn't normally be comfortable extrapolating it to the whole situation of the column, but it's not inconsistent with other stories that I've heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go back to P329, please. And this time, I'm interested in you looking at a paragraph below the two that we have been concentrating on thus far: "I made an offer to the commander of the other side to separate out civilians and have the others surrender, but he refused, asking that they should all be released together." Do you have any reason to doubt the veracity of that assertion in a document written at about 7.00 p.m. on the 15th of July, that by then, Vinko Pandurevic had already made an offer to allow people to pass and to surrender?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, and I -- I believe that I have heard, either in statements or whatever, you know, similar language from the ABiH side, because their, of course, primary concern is they didn't want to be in a situation where they were parsing out between their soldiers and the civilians. They wanted everyone out, and so, in part, they weren't going to accept that, because what the VRS was asking was unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I know that you're aware that by mid-afternoon on the 15th of July, all units of the Zvornik Brigade were back in position to fight the column. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be a matter of timing. I know the last units getting in place were the Drina Wolves and -- I think the police units actually got there before the Drina Wolves did, so, I mean, most of them were certainly, by the time the sun was going down, they were in positions where they could substantially contribute.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you've listed in your reports the many and various reinforcements from other areas that were sent to help them as well, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But I want to know what your knowledge of the artillery capability of the Zvornik Brigade was on the afternoon of the 15th and morning of 16th of July. Did you have any awareness of that when you wrote your report or as you sit here today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I have a general awareness, and it wasn't very much, but, no, I can't tell you that I specifically examined the details of the artillery units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In order not to go into private session, nor to compromise anybody, I'm going to read to you something that PW-168 said in, in fact, his proofing session. He said -- he briefly recounted his previous statements regarding the opening of the corridor for the column to pass: "The witness reiterated that this was Pandurevic's decision. The witness went on to state that Pandurevic could have withdrawn his troops from the battlefield area on the 16th of July and showered the Muslim groups in the area with full artillery, killing many more of them, but instead Pandurevic chose to allow the column to pass for 28 hours before closing the corridor." Had you read that or considered any evidence to that effect before coming to the conclusions you did in your report or in your evidence before this Court?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, the phrase "full artillery" I think within the context of the Zvornik Brigade is not much, but certainly, yeah, Colonel Pandurevic had an option where he could do that at that juncture, if he chose to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You were asked a question by Mr. McCloskey. I'm going to ask you a couple. Knowing now that the numbers of dead are suggested to be far fewer than you thought, that the conditions that the column was in were terrible, that there were offers to let them go on the 15th of July, and that he could have withdrawn his troops and showered the column with artillery and killed thousands of them, do you want to revise your views as to his motivations for letting the column pass?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Revise them from what? I mean, what do you attribute my view as to letting the -- what do you attribute to be my view of his motivation for letting the column pass?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I think you said earlier on in your evidence that he pretty much had to let them go. Do you stand by that or do you not suggest that anymore?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no, I stand by that. I mean, sure, could -- could the AB -- the Muslim -- the Serb forces tried to withdraw and get enough clearance that the Muslims could have, you know, gone out and then showered them with artillery fire, in abstract. Would the Muslims have allowed them to engage once they saw that happening and do that? No. I mean, the Muslims understood that, you know, their best chance of survival with respect to indirect fire was to be in as close contact with the VRS as possible so they wouldn't shoot. I stand by my analysis, that when I look at this material, I mean, he made the decision to let the column go based on the factors that he had available to him at the time. He concluded he had no choice, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: He also concluded that it would be better not to kill thousands more of the Muslims in the column, didn't he, according to what I've just read to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, I was looking at this, not -- not -- I take it what you read to me, you were referring to PW-168.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly that witness attributes that motive to him. I mean, I don't know that as a fact or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, and he was on the ground, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, I'm not going to parse that particular motive. I just don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And he presumably knew better than you do what the artillery capability of the Zvornik Brigade was on the 16th of July, 1995, and you don't, do you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment, I will certainly grant him that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The other question Mr. McCloskey asked you was whether you saw any evidence of Pandurevic standing up to Mladic in relation to the killing operation. Isn't his decision not to withdraw his troops and shower the column and kill thousands of them just that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Let's redact that. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, at this time, before moving on to redirect from the Prosecution, I would like to seek leave from the Trial Chamber for a short extended cross-examination arising from the questions that were posed by my colleague. I've got four specific and short questions which arise from the questions that were put by my colleague at lines 15 [sic], 10 to 25, lines 10 to 25 and lines -- and page 12, lines 9 to 24. So two questions that were put by my colleague, and I'd like to have leave to do some further cross-examination with four specific and short questions to clarify these issues, in the interests both of clarifying and for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think perhaps it's best if I go next. I, too, wish to ask some further questions. They relate to the document the witness has brought to court today. I suspect it will take no more than two or three minutes. It's really a rather different application to Mr. Bourgon's, but I better put it on the record at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We have met repeatedly about the evidence of this witness and been fairly candid about the topics of cross-examination we were going to employ. I went first for a considerable time with another substantial witness in this case, and others were allowed to cross-examine after me, and I lived with that. I object to anybody having the right to further cross-examination. There's an indictment order. It's a multi-handed case. These things happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd spoken to Mr. Josse about the issue he spoke of, which I think is something that we agree that needed to be cleared up as one of the items I think the Court is familiar with, so no problem. Given the cross and the -- if there are specific areas Mr. Bourgon, as he says he has, I don't object to short, specific -- just a few to clear up those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, one moment. We haven't given you the go-ahead as yet, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bourgon, could you tell us first what your first questions are, please, what your two or four questions are?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to do, Mr. President. First, the -- the first question has to do with the information which can be provided to the commander by the assistant commander for security, and this arises from a question that was put by my colleague on page 12 of the transcript. Now, I might not have the right page, because I think they started again the numeration of pages. That was on page 12, lines 9 to 24. The questions was at lines 9 to 12, and the answer was at lines 13 to 24. So my first two questions deal with what kind of information can be put by the security officer to his commanding officer. So that's the first two questions. And the next two questions deal with the measures which can be taken by the brigade commander if he believes that his security officer has committed a crime. And that was raised specifically by my colleague at page 15, lines 10 to 25, and page 16, lines 1 to 3; four specific and short questions with no more than five minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: First observation: All asked and answered in his first cross-examination. Secondly, bring it as part of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our decision is as follows, and it's unanimous: In relation to your request, Mr. Bourgon, our conviction is that the areas you wish to cover have already been covered sufficiently, in our minds, in a way that does not require any further clarification. So we are dismissing your request. In regard to Mr. Josse, we see the importance of clarification, particularly because this document came to the surface only today, and so you are allowed two minutes to conclude. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I would like to seek certification of this decision from the Trial Chamber on the basis of past practice before this Trial Chamber, which this decision I feel is different, and I would like to know if you wish me to do this orally or in writing, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If he comes over and talks to me afterward, maybe we can avoid certification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll deal with that after you have spoken. If you wish to speak to Mr. McCloskey, of course we are not imposing any such requirement. But if you bring this up again tomorrow, we'll tell you whether you need to raise it orally or in writing. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
